title: Psalm 40: A New Song and a Willing Heart
summary: David recalls waiting patiently for the LORD, who drew him out of the pit and gave him a new song. He declares that God desires not sacrifice alone but a heart that delights to do his will, and he has proclaimed God's righteousness in the great assembly. Then, surrounded again by troubles and sins, he pleads for help and asks God not to delay.
story: Psalm 39 ended in unresolved waiting. Psalm 40 opens with waiting that has been answered: I waited patiently for the LORD, and he heard. It is two kinds of psalm joined together: a thanksgiving (verses 1 to 10) and a lament (verses 11 to 17). Its movement from rescue back to need reflects real life, where one deliverance doesn't end all trouble. The psalm matters in the larger story because Hebrews 10 quotes verses 6 to 8 as words of Christ entering the world, making this one of the key Old Testament passages for understanding why Jesus came.
historical:
The heading attributes the psalm to David and directs it to the choirmaster. No specific event is named. Verses 13 to 17 appear, with small differences, as a separate psalm, Psalm 70, and scholars debate how the two relate: whether Psalm 40 combined an older thanksgiving with an existing lament, or whether its closing section was later detached for separate use. Such reuse of material is common in the Psalter (Psalm 53 closely repeats Psalm 14, and Psalm 108 combines parts of Psalms 57 and 60).

The reference in verse 7 to the scroll where it is written about me has been read in several ways. Some connect it with the law's instruction that Israel's king write for himself a copy of the law and read it all his life (Deuteronomy 17:18-20), so that a royal speaker would find his calling described in Torah. Others take it more broadly as the written word of God that directs the speaker's life.
cultural:
The pit and miry clay of verse 2 recall a common feature of ancient Israel: cisterns cut into rock to store rainwater. When empty they held mud at the bottom and were sometimes used as prisons; Joseph was thrown into one (Genesis 37:24), and Jeremiah was lowered into one and sank in the mud (Jeremiah 38:6). Being set on a rock was the opposite of that helplessness.

The list of offerings in verse 6 names the main types of Israelite sacrifice: sacrifice (animal offerings shared in a meal), offering (grain offerings), burnt offerings (wholly burned), and sin offerings (for purification from sin). The statement that God didn't desire or require them echoes the prophets (1 Samuel 15:22; Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6-8). These passages are generally understood not as rejecting sacrifice entirely but as saying that ritual without obedience is worthless to God. The great assembly of verses 9 and 10 was the gathered congregation at the temple, where individual thanksgivings were spoken publicly.
literary: The first half is thanksgiving, with vivid rescue imagery: waiting, crying, lifting, setting feet on a rock, giving a new song. Verses 4 and 5 widen into a beatitude and a hymn to God's countless wonders. The center, verses 6 to 8, is the psalm's theological heart, contrasting ritual with obedience and quoting the speaker's own words of self-offering. Verses 9 and 10 use a cluster of verbs of speaking and not concealing, as though the psalmist is insisting that his thanks have been public. Then verse 11 turns to plea, and verses 12 to 17 are an urgent lament. The shift is jarring, but it holds together through repeated words: countless wonders in verse 5 and evils without number in verse 12, loving devotion and faithfulness in verses 10 and 11.

outline.t: Drawn out of the pit and given a new song
Blessing on the one who trusts; God's countless wonders
Not sacrifice alone but a heart that delights in God's will
God's righteousness proclaimed in the great assembly
Surrounded again by evils and sins
Hurry to help me: a plea for rescue

doctrines.note: Verses 6 to 8 say that animal sacrifices are not what God finally desires. Hebrews 10 reads this as fulfilled when Christ offered himself, doing God's will perfectly and making the old sacrifices obsolete.

Your law is within my heart (verse 8) describes obedience that comes from inside, not only outward compliance. It anticipates the new covenant promise that God will write his law on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33).
The psalm shows that a person rescued once may need rescuing again. Thanksgiving and lament belong together in a life of prayer.

words.note: Qavah, to wait. The psalm opens with the verb doubled in Hebrew, which the BSB renders I waited patiently. The doubling intensifies the idea: waiting and waiting, or waiting with determination. It is the same verb used in Psalm 37:9 and 37:34 for those who hope in the LORD.

Ozen, ear. Verse 6 says literally ears You have dug for me, which the BSB renders my ears You have opened. The picture may be of God opening the ears to hear and obey. The Septuagint reads instead a body You prepared for me, and Hebrews 10:5 follows that Greek reading. Both versions make the same point: God wants the whole self given in obedience.

Megillah, scroll. In verse 7 the speaker says it is written about him in the scroll. The word later names the five scrolls read at Jewish festivals (such as Esther). Here it most likely refers to the written law, where the speaker finds his life's calling described.

christ: Hebrews 10:5-10 quotes verses 6 to 8 as the words of Christ when he came into the world. The writer argues that God did not finally desire animal sacrifices, which could not take away sins, but a perfect obedience, which Jesus offered in his own body. Following the Greek text, Hebrews reads a body You prepared for me, and sees in that line the incarnation itself. So the psalm's willing servant, who delights to do God's will and has God's law in his heart, is fulfilled in Jesus, whose self-offering made the old sacrifices unnecessary. That is an explicit New Testament reading, not an invented one. At the same time, the psalm's later confession of sins (verse 12) shows that its original speaker was an ordinary sinner, not the sinless Christ; Hebrews applies to Jesus the part of the psalm that describes perfect obedience.

hard.q: Hebrews quotes this psalm with different words. Did the writer misquote it?
hard.a: Verse 6 in Hebrew says, literally, ears You have dug for me. Hebrews 10:5 quotes it as a body You prepared for me, following the Greek Septuagint, the translation most early Christians used. Scholars discuss how the Greek reading arose: some suggest the translators interpreted the opening of the ears as the preparing of the whole body for obedience, a part standing for the whole; others propose a copying change in the Greek manuscripts. The writer of Hebrews quoted the version his readers knew, and his argument doesn't depend on the difference. Both readings make the same point: God wants the obedience of the whole person, not ritual alone. Christians hold that the New Testament writers used their Scriptures faithfully even when quoting from translations, and that the Holy Spirit's intent is carried by both forms.

questions: The psalm opens with patient waiting that God answered. What are you waiting for, and what helps you wait patiently?
Verses 6 to 8 say God wants a heart that delights to do his will more than religious ritual. Where might you be offering God the ritual without the heart?
The psalm moves from thanksgiving back into need. How does remembering past rescue help you face present trouble?
